sections.section_title: Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism

content_groups.group_title: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) and Pulmonary Embolism (PE)

blocks.text: Prescription & Medication Guide · Treatment-focused clinical reference

Venous thromboembolism (VTE) comprises deep vein thrombosis, in which a thrombus forms in the deep venous system, and pulmonary embolism, in which thrombotic material obstructs the pulmonary arteries. Treatment aims to prevent clot extension, recurrent embolism and death while minimising bleeding.

Critical safety principle: Suspected high-risk PE with shock or persistent hypotension is a medical emergency. Stabilisation, urgent specialist involvement and consideration of reperfusion must not be delayed by routine investigations. Anticoagulant choice and dose depend on haemodynamic status, renal function, body weight, pregnancy, bleeding risk, drug interactions and local availability.

rows: Anticoagulation or serial ultrasound in selected low-risk cases
Popliteal, femoral or iliac vein involvement
Therapeutic anticoagulation, generally for at least 3 months
Haemodynamically stable, low predicted short-term risk
Anticoagulation; outpatient treatment only after structured risk assessment
Stable blood pressure but evidence of right ventricular strain and/or myocardial injury
Hospital observation or admission; monitor for deterioration
Cardiac arrest, obstructive shock or persistent hypotension attributable to PE
Emergency resuscitation, IV anticoagulation and consideration of reperfusion

blocks.text: A confirmed proximal DVT or PE generally requires at least 3 months of anticoagulation. The decision to continue beyond that point depends on the provoking factor, recurrence risk, bleeding risk and patient preferences.

subsections.subsection_title: 2. When admission or urgent specialist care is needed

blocks.title: Admit urgently or manage in an appropriately monitored setting when there is:

items.text: Haemodynamic instability, syncope with ongoing concern, hypoxaemia or suspected high-risk PE.
Right ventricular dysfunction, myocardial injury or clinical deterioration.
Significant bleeding risk, active bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia or a complex anticoagulation decision.
Severe renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy with acute VTE, suspected recurrent VTE despite treatment, or a need for an urgent procedure.
Extensive iliofemoral thrombosis with severe symptoms or threatened limb viability.
Unreliable medication access, inability to take oral medication, or inadequate support for safe outpatient treatment.

blocks.text: Outpatient treatment may be appropriate for carefully selected low-risk PE or DVT patients only if stability, bleeding risk, comorbidities, medication access and reliable follow-up have been assessed.

items.text: Prevent clot extension and recurrent DVT or PE.
Reduce PE-related mortality and haemodynamic deterioration.
Relieve symptoms and preserve limb function.
Minimise major bleeding and drug-related complications.
Determine an appropriate treatment duration and prevent recurrence.

blocks.title: Obtain baseline investigations as soon as feasible:

items.text: Full blood count, including haemoglobin and platelet count.
Renal function, ideally calculated creatinine clearance when required for anticoagulant dosing.
Liver function.
PT/INR and aPTT.
Pregnancy test where relevant.
Additional tests guided by severity, including troponin, BNP/NT-proBNP, ECG, echocardiography and blood gas analysis in selected PE cases.

blocks.text: Do not delay urgently indicated anticoagulation solely while awaiting routine baseline blood results, provided there is no contraindication that would make treatment unsafe. If imaging is delayed and clinical probability is sufficiently high, interim therapeutic anticoagulation may be indicated after assessing bleeding risk.
**Pathway 1 — Stable adult with confirmed DVT or PE**
Usually use apixaban or rivaroxaban when appropriate, or select a heparin-based pathway followed by dabigatran, edoxaban or warfarin.
Resuscitation and critical care; IV unfractionated heparin (UFH) is commonly used when haemodynamically unstable, with urgent assessment for systemic thrombolysis or another reperfusion strategy.
Use a pregnancy-appropriate anticoagulation pathway, generally low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH); do not routinely use DOACs.

content_groups.group_title: Pathway 4 — Severe renal impairment or complex comorbidity

blocks.text: Individualise the choice; UFH and/or warfarin may be appropriate. Follow product-specific renal restrictions and specialist guidance.

The following are standard adult treatment regimens, not prophylactic doses. Confirm the indication, creatinine clearance, weight, interactions, bleeding risk and local product information before prescribing.
**Apixaban**
Direct factor Xa inhibitor · Oral
Common first-line option
Initial treatment: 10 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days.
Then: 5 mg orally every 12 hours.
Duration: Usually at least 3 months; reassess the need for extended treatment.
Extended prevention: For selected adults who have completed at least 6 months of treatment, 2.5 mg orally every 12 hours may be used for prevention of recurrent DVT/PE.
Do not apply atrial-fibrillation dose-reduction criteria to the acute VTE treatment regimen.
**Example prescription — initial 7-day phase**
Rx
Apixaban 5 mg tablets
Take 2 tablets orally every 12 hours for 7 days.
Quantity: 28 tablets for the initial phase.
Dispense and document the subsequent maintenance prescription separately: apixaban 5 mg orally every 12 hours.
**Key cautions**

items.text: Active major bleeding is a contraindication.
Review renal and hepatic function, concurrent antiplatelets/NSAIDs and strong P-glycoprotein/CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers.
Avoid or seek specialist advice in severe hepatic disease with coagulopathy and in severe renal impairment according to local product labelling.
Routine INR monitoring does not measure apixaban effect reliably.

blocks.text: **B. Rivaroxaban**
Direct factor Xa inhibitor · Oral
Initial treatment: 15 mg orally every 12 hours for 21 days, taken with food.
Then: 20 mg orally once daily with food.
Extended prevention: In selected adults after at least 6 months of standard treatment, 10 mg once daily may be considered; continued 20 mg once daily may be appropriate when recurrence risk is high.
**Example prescription — initial 21-day phase**
Rx
Rivaroxaban 15 mg tablets
Take 1 tablet orally every 12 hours with food for 21 days.
Quantity: 42 tablets.
On day 22, transition to the prescribed maintenance regimen, usually 20 mg orally once daily with food.
**Key cautions**

items.text: The 15 mg and 20 mg doses must be taken with food.
Assess renal function and follow the product-specific creatinine-clearance restrictions.
Avoid strong combined P-glycoprotein/CYP3A4 inducers and review strong inhibitors.
Do not use for VTE treatment in pregnancy; avoid routine use during breastfeeding without specialist advice.

blocks.text: **C. Dabigatran**
Dabigatran is not normally started as the sole initial drug for acute VTE.

items.text: Give therapeutic parenteral anticoagulation for 5–10 days first.
Then, for most eligible adults, dabigatran 150 mg orally every 12 hours.
Check renal function carefully; dabigatran is highly dependent on renal clearance.
Age, bleeding risk, interacting medicines and local licensing may change eligibility or dosing.

blocks.text: **D. Edoxaban**

items.text: Give therapeutic parenteral anticoagulation for at least 5 days first.
Standard adult dose: 60 mg orally once daily.

The dose is generally reduced to 30 mg once daily for creatinine clearance 15–50 mL/min, body weight 60 kg or less, or certain relevant P-glycoprotein inhibitors, according to the applicable product label.
Avoid where renal function is below the licensed threshold; verify the current local product information.

blocks.text: Clinical point: Apixaban and rivaroxaban use a higher-dose oral initiation phase. Dabigatran and edoxaban require a preceding parenteral anticoagulant phase. These regimens are not interchangeable.
Common adult therapeutic regimens

items.text: 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours; or
1.5 mg/kg subcutaneously once daily in selected patients.
For severe renal impairment, a commonly used adjustment is 1 mg/kg subcutaneously once daily when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min. Follow the applicable product label and local protocol.
In pregnancy, cancer-associated VTE, severe obesity or high-risk PE, use an appropriate specialist pathway.

blocks.text: **Worked example: Adult weighing 70 kg, normal renal function.**
Example prescription — enoxaparin 1 mg/kg every 12 hours
Enoxaparin 70 mg subcutaneously every 12 hours.
Calculated dose: \(70\text{ kg}\times1\text{ mg/kg}=70\text{ mg}\).
If the available prefilled syringe permits accurate measurement of 70 mg, administer that dose. Verify the syringe concentration and device instructions before dispensing.
**Contraindications and precautions**

items.text: Active major bleeding; previous or current heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT); severe thrombocytopenia; recent high-risk surgery or intracranial bleeding.
Use caution in renal impairment, low body weight, obesity, pregnancy, and when neuraxial anaesthesia or spinal procedures are planned.
Do not inject intramuscularly.
Monitor full blood count, renal function and bleeding. Anti-Xa measurement is reserved for selected situations under a local protocol; it is not required routinely for every patient.

blocks.text: UFH is especially useful when PE is haemodynamically unstable, renal impairment is severe, rapid adjustment may be needed, or an urgent procedure or reperfusion treatment is anticipated.
**Administration**

items.text: Use a hospital-approved, weight-based IV bolus and infusion protocol.
Titrate against the institution's therapeutic aPTT or anti-Xa target.
Obtain baseline aPTT, full blood count and platelet count; monitor according to the infusion protocol.
Dosing protocols vary by institution and indication. Do not use a fixed infusion rate without the required weight-based calculation and laboratory monitoring.

blocks.text: **Adverse effects**: Bleeding, HIT, thrombocytopenia and, with prolonged exposure, osteoporosis.

**Reversal**: Protamine sulfate can reverse UFH. Administer according to the amount of heparin recently received and the local reversal protocol; rapid administration can cause serious hypotension and anaphylactoid reactions.
A weight-based adult subcutaneous regimen sometimes used for acute VTE is:
Avoid in severe renal impairment according to product labelling. It is not the routine choice for unstable PE, and suspected or confirmed HIT requires specialist-directed anticoagulant selection.
Warfarin may be used where DOACs are unsuitable, unaffordable or unavailable, and is often preferred for certain conditions such as triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome.
**Starting treatment**

items.text: Start warfarin alongside a therapeutic parenteral anticoagulant.
Continue the parenteral anticoagulant for at least 5 days and until the INR is therapeutic according to the local protocol—commonly INR 2.0–3.0, confirmed by the required consecutive readings.
Continue warfarin alone once overlap criteria are met.
Adjust the dose according to INR results, clinical factors and the local anticoagulation service.

blocks.text: Do not prescribe a universal fixed warfarin maintenance dose. The appropriate starting and maintenance dose depends on age, liver function, diet, interacting medicines, bleeding risk and INR response.

**Important interactions**: Antibiotics, azole antifungals, amiodarone, many antiepileptics, alcohol changes and substantial dietary changes may alter INR. A newly prescribed or discontinued medicine should prompt an interaction check and an appropriate INR plan.

**Pregnancy**: Warfarin is generally avoided for ordinary pregnancy-associated VTE; management must be directed by an obstetric and haematology team. Warfarin can generally be used during breastfeeding.
High-risk PE may cause obstructive shock, cardiac arrest and rapid death. This is not managed as an uncomplicated outpatient VTE.

items.text: Resuscitate and provide oxygen or ventilatory support when indicated.
Obtain urgent critical care and specialist input.
Use IV UFH when appropriate under the local PE protocol.
Assess for urgent reperfusion, usually systemic thrombolysis where indicated; catheter-directed treatment or surgical embolectomy may be alternatives where available and appropriate.

blocks.text: A commonly used adult systemic thrombolysis regimen is:
Alteplase 100 mg IV infused over 2 hours.

This is a hospital emergency regimen for appropriately selected patients—not routine treatment for a haemodynamically stable PE. Confirm the indication, bleeding risk, contraindications, product instructions and local protocol before administration.

blocks.title: **Major contraindications or red flags for thrombolysis include:**

items.text: Previous haemorrhagic stroke or stroke of unknown origin.
Recent ischaemic stroke.
Active bleeding or a known bleeding diathesis.
Recent intracranial or spinal surgery, significant head trauma or other major bleeding-risk conditions.

blocks.text: The precise contraindication list and how to weigh relative contraindications depend on the current protocol and the urgency of the clinical situation.

After thrombolysis: Monitor closely for intracranial and other major bleeding, neurological change and haemodynamic response. Restart or continue anticoagulation according to the post-thrombolysis protocol and coagulation results. Do not automatically administer another anticoagulant bolus without checking the timing and relevant laboratory parameters.

content_groups.group_title: Is thrombolysis indicated for every PE?

blocks.text: No. Routine systemic thrombolysis is not recommended for every haemodynamically stable PE, because bleeding risk can outweigh benefit. Stable patients are generally treated with anticoagulation, with escalation if clinical deterioration occurs.

rows: Proximal DVT or PE provoked by a temporary risk factor that has resolved
Consider extended treatment if recurrence risk outweighs bleeding risk
Treat for at least 3–6 months and reassess; continuation may be needed while cancer or treatment-related risk persists
Often extended or indefinite treatment, depending on the circumstances
Anticoagulation or serial ultrasound depending on extension risk, symptoms and bleeding risk

blocks.text: For a first event clearly provoked by a resolved transient risk factor, stopping after 3 months may be reasonable if the course is uncomplicated. For unprovoked events or persistent risk factors, the decision to continue should balance recurrence against bleeding and be reviewed periodically.
Important: A lower-dose extended-prevention regimen is not a substitute for the full initial treatment regimen.

items.text: Pregnancy: LMWH is generally preferred for treatment of acute VTE. A common therapeutic enoxaparin regimen is 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours, subject to renal function and specialist review.
DOACs: Avoid routine use during pregnancy; they are also generally avoided during breastfeeding because of limited safety data and guideline concerns.
Warfarin: Generally avoided for ordinary pregnancy-associated VTE, but may be used during breastfeeding under appropriate management.
Continue anticoagulation for at least 3 months in total and for at least 6 weeks postpartum, whichever requires the longer course, under an obstetric anticoagulation plan.
Coordinate delivery, interruption and resumption of anticoagulation, and neuraxial anaesthesia with the obstetric and anaesthetic teams.

rows: Select the anticoagulant and dose using the relevant product label and calculated creatinine clearance
Some DOACs may be used with restrictions; dabigatran and edoxaban have specific limitations
Specialist-led choice; UFH and/or warfarin may be appropriate
Reassess dosing promptly; drug accumulation can cause bleeding

blocks.text: Do not assume that all DOACs have the same renal restrictions. For drug dosing, estimated creatinine clearance using the method specified by the product label may be more appropriate than relying on a laboratory-reported eGFR alone.

blocks.title: A DOAC or LMWH may be appropriate. Consider:

items.text: Tumour site, especially gastrointestinal or genitourinary cancers with increased bleeding risk.
Drug interactions with anticancer medicines.
Thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, absorption problems and planned procedures.
Patient preference, cost, availability and ability to adhere.

blocks.text: For triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome, a vitamin K antagonist such as warfarin is generally preferred over a DOAC. Refer for specialist management.

Paediatric VTE treatment requires a dedicated paediatric protocol. Dosing varies with age, weight, renal function, formulation and the chosen anticoagulant. Do not automatically apply adult DOAC regimens to children. Specialist guidance should define weight-based dosing, monitoring and duration.

For patients weighing less than 50 kg or more than 120 kg, check the specific drug label and local protocol. Consider specialist input and drug-level monitoring where appropriate; DOAC, LMWH and UFH considerations differ.

Major bleeding requires immediate assessment, withholding the anticoagulant when appropriate, resuscitation, source control and urgent specialist input. Check the last dose, renal function, interacting medicines, blood count and relevant coagulation tests.

rows: Protamine provides partial reversal; effectiveness depends on timing and dose
Vitamin K plus four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) for life-threatening bleeding where available; follow emergency protocol
Andexanet alfa where available and appropriate, or a protocol-directed PCC strategy

blocks.text: Availability of specific reversal agents varies by facility and country. Do not delay emergency supportive care while sourcing a reversal drug.

Do not use a normal PT/INR or aPTT to conclude that a patient taking a DOAC has no clinically significant anticoagulant effect. Standard clotting tests may not reliably quantify the effect of these medicines.

content_groups.group_title: Important contraindications or situations requiring specialist review

items.text: Active major bleeding.
Recent intracranial haemorrhage or high-risk intracranial lesion.
Severe thrombocytopenia or suspected HIT.
Severe renal or hepatic impairment affecting the selected drug.
Pregnancy or breastfeeding when considering a DOAC.
Recent surgery, trauma, neuraxial procedure or planned invasive intervention.
Concurrent use of other anticoagulants or multiple antiplatelet agents without a clear indication.

rows: Increased bleeding risk when combined with anticoagulation
May increase apixaban or rivaroxaban exposure
May reduce DOAC exposure and treatment effectiveness
Antibiotics and azole antifungals with warfarin
INR may rise or fall; monitor closely
INR may increase; reassess warfarin dosing and monitoring

blocks.text: Always check the exact interaction against the specific anticoagulant and the patient's complete medication list.

content_groups.group_title: Before discharge or transition to outpatient treatment

items.text: Confirm the anticoagulant, dose, frequency and planned duration.
Ensure the patient has the medication supply needed to complete the initial phase without interruption.
Check renal function, haemoglobin and platelet results as clinically appropriate.
Establish a plan for follow-up, laboratory monitoring and review of bleeding risk.
Confirm that the patient understands any transition from a loading regimen to a maintenance regimen.

rows: Within the first few days when clinically indicated
Confirm tolerance, adherence, access to medication and review of baseline results
Reassess symptoms, bleeding, renal function where relevant and correct dosing
Review provoking factors, recurrence risk, bleeding risk and whether anticoagulation should stop or continue
Periodic reassessment of renal/hepatic function, bleeding risk, interactions and ongoing indication

blocks.text: The timing should be individualised, especially for frail patients, those with renal impairment, active cancer or changing clinical status.
Suspect treatment failure if symptoms worsen or new symptoms suggest recurrent DVT or PE despite prescribed anticoagulation.

items.text: Confirm the diagnosis with appropriate imaging where indicated.
Check adherence, missed doses, correct initial dosing and access to medication.
Review interactions that may reduce anticoagulant exposure.
Reassess renal function, malignancy and other prothrombotic conditions.
Obtain specialist advice before increasing the dose or switching anticoagulants.

blocks.text: Do not automatically increase an anticoagulant dose without establishing the likely reason for recurrence.

Inferior vena cava (IVC) filter: Not routinely indicated when anticoagulation can be given. Consider only in selected circumstances, such as a contraindication to anticoagulation, or recurrent PE despite adequate anticoagulation after treatment failure has been carefully assessed. A retrievable filter should have a documented plan for reassessment and removal.

Catheter-directed treatment or surgical embolectomy: May be considered in selected patients with severe PE or DVT, particularly when thrombolysis is contraindicated, has failed or another intervention is judged more appropriate by the specialist team.
Compression stockings: May help selected patients with leg symptoms, but should not be prescribed routinely solely to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome.

blocks.title: Explain the following in language the patient understands:

items.text: Take the anticoagulant exactly as prescribed. Do not stop it or double a missed dose without following the medicine-specific instructions.
Seek emergency care for severe breathlessness, chest pain, collapse, coughing up significant blood, severe headache, new neurological symptoms, vomiting blood, black stools or uncontrolled bleeding.
Report unusual bruising, persistent nosebleeds, blood in urine or other signs of bleeding promptly.
Check before starting new medicines, particularly NSAIDs, aspirin, herbal products or antibiotics.
Inform healthcare professionals and dentists about anticoagulant use before procedures.
Discuss pregnancy planning and contraception where relevant.
Keep follow-up appointments and do not run out of medication.
Encourage appropriate mobilisation when clinically safe; avoid prolonged immobility and follow advice on travel and recurrence prevention.

blocks.text: Confusing prophylaxis with treatment
Prophylactic enoxaparin doses are not adequate treatment for established DVT or PE.
Omitting the initial DOAC phase
Apixaban and rivaroxaban require their specific initial treatment regimens for acute VTE.
Incorrect transition to maintenance dosing
For rivaroxaban, the initial phase lasts 21 days; for apixaban, 7 days. Write the transition date clearly.
Starting dabigatran or edoxaban without initial parenteral treatment
These acute VTE regimens require a preceding therapeutic parenteral anticoagulant phase.
Failing to reassess treatment duration
Every patient should have an explicit plan to review whether anticoagulation should stop or continue.

items.text: DVT and PE are manifestations of the same disease process: assess for the other manifestation when clinically indicated.
A normal D-dimer is most useful when pre-test probability is low or unlikely and an appropriate diagnostic pathway is being followed.
A haemodynamically unstable PE is a reperfusion emergency, not simply an indication for routine oral anticoagulation.
Apixaban and rivaroxaban can be started orally using their designated initial regimens in eligible stable adults; dabigatran and edoxaban require preceding parenteral anticoagulation.
Warfarin requires overlap with a therapeutic parenteral anticoagulant during initiation for acute VTE.
Pregnancy-associated VTE is generally treated with LMWH, not a DOAC.
The minimum treatment duration for proximal DVT or PE is usually 3 months, followed by an individualised recurrence-versus-bleeding assessment.
Breakthrough VTE requires a systematic review of adherence, dosing, interactions and underlying risk factors before changing treatment.
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence — Venous thromboembolic diseases: diagnosis, management and thrombophilia testing.
European Society of Cardiology — Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism.

blocks.text: Prescribing note: This chapter is a clinical reference, not a substitute for patient-specific prescribing. Confirm current product labelling, renal dosing, contraindications and locally available reversal agents before treatment.
